t: Find Pattern in Infinite Stream I — Rolling Hash over a Live Stream
o: We read bits one at a time from an infinite stream and must report the starting index of the first window of length m = pattern.length whose bits equal the pattern. Since the stream is infinite, we cannot buffer it all; we must decide as we go. Example 1: reading 1,1,1,0,1..., the first window [0,1] appears at index 3. Example 2: pattern [0] matches immediately at index 0. Example 3: pattern [1,1,0,1] first matches starting at index 2. Constraints (m ≤ 100, answer within the first 10^5 bits) mean even a naive per-window comparison is fine (~10^7 ops), but a rolling hash gives a clean O(n) solution that also scales to harder variants.
k: Treat each incoming bit as extending a sliding window of length m; compare the window to the pattern only once it is full.
A rolling hash lets us update the window fingerprint in O(1) per new bit instead of re-hashing or re-comparing the whole window.
Because the match is guaranteed within the first 10^5 bits, we can loop until found without any termination worry.

a.i: Keep the last m bits in a deque/buffer. Once we have read at least m bits, compare the buffer element-by-element with the pattern. With m ≤ 100 and n ≤ 10^5 this is at most ~10^7 comparisons, well within limits. It is the most direct translation of the problem statement.
s: Initialize an empty list buffer and index counter i = 0.
Read bit b = stream.next(); append b to buffer; increment i.
If buffer size exceeds m, pop from the front.
When buffer size equals m, check if buffer == pattern; if yes return i - m.
Repeat until a match is found.
a.t: O(n·m) time — each of up to n reads triggers an O(m) comparison in the worst case; fine since n ≤ 10^5 and m ≤ 100.
a.sp: O(m) space for the sliding buffer.

a.i: Maintain a polynomial hash of the current window: hash = sum(bit_j * base^(m-1-j)) mod MOD. When a new bit arrives, drop the oldest bit's contribution by subtracting old * base^(m-1), multiply by base, and add the new bit — all O(1). Compare the rolling hash against the precomputed pattern hash; on equality, verify once directly to guard against collisions (or use double hashing). This yields linear time regardless of m.
s: Precompute pattern hash hp = fold bits with base B modulo MOD, and power = B^(m-1) mod MOD.
Read bits one at a time, keeping hash h of the last min(i, m) bits and count c.
For each new bit b: h = (h*B + b) % MOD; if c == m, remove oldest: h = (h - oldest*power % MOD + MOD) % MOD using a queue of window bits.
When c == m and h == hp, verify the window against the pattern directly (collision safety) and return start index if equal.
Continue until a verified match is found.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def findPattern(self, stream: 'InfiniteStream', pattern: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD, BASE = (1 << 61) - 1, 131
        m = len(pattern)
        hp = 0
        for b in pattern:
            hp = (hp * BASE + b) % MOD
        power = pow(BASE, m - 1, MOD)
        h, c, start = 0, 0, 0
        win = []
        i = 0
        while True:
            b = stream.next()
            h = (h * BASE + b) % MOD
            if c == m:
                h = (h - win[0] * power) % MOD
                win.pop(0)
                start += 1
            else:
                c += 1
            win.append(b)
            i += 1
            if c == m and h == hp and win == pattern:
                return start

a.t: O(n + m) time — one O(1) hash update per streamed bit plus O(m) preprocessing and at most one O(m) verification.
a.sp: O(m) space for the window buffer and stored bits.

w: In an interview, lead with the brute-force buffer approach to establish correctness quickly, then upgrade to rolling hash to show streaming awareness — the optimal choice when m is large or the stream is truly unbounded. Pitfalls: off-by-one on the start index (return i - m, not i); forgetting to handle negative values after modular subtraction in C++/Java; forgetting collision verification if using a small modulus. Edge cases: pattern length 1 (matches at first occurrence of that bit), pattern of all zeros vs all-ones streams. Follow-ups: LeetCode 3024 asks for pattern length up to 10^5, where KMP or Z-algorithm over the live stream becomes relevant; you may also be asked why hashing beats direct comparison asymptotically.
